In this chapter, the rock magnetic properties of sediments will be summarized briefly with respect to their mineralogy, particulary of red beds and types of remanence. Although no specific rock magnetic studies have been carried out, a general overview is thought to be relevant for the results obtained. For a more extensive discussion of palaeomagnetism and rock magnetism, see Nagata (1961), Irving (1964), Stacey and Banerjee (L974) and McElhinny (1973). The main points are summarized below. 1. In sedimentary rocks, haematite is one of the most stable magnetic phase under oxidising conditions (O’Reilly, 1976) and can be of both syn- and post-depositional origin in red beds. Other types of sedimentary rocks such as varved clays may more directly reflect mineralogy related to the source material in the bed rock terrain and can be expected to contain both haematite and magnetite as detrital minerals. 2. The total Natural Remanent Magnetization (NRM) of rocks is commonly a vector sum of several different types of remanent magnetization. For a more extensive discussion of palaeomagnetism and rock magnetism, see Nagata (1961), Irving (1964), Stacey and Banerjee (L974) and McElhinny (1973). The main points are summarized below. 1. In sedimentary rocks, haematite is one of the most stable magnetic phase under oxidising conditions (O’Reilly, 1976) and can be of both syn- and post-depositional origin in red beds. Other types of sedimentary rocks such as varved clays may more directly reflect mineralogy related to the source material in the bed rock terrain and can be expected to contain both haematite and magnetite as detrital minerals. 2. The total Natural Remanent Magnetization (NRM) of rocks is commonly a vector sum of several different types of remanent magnetization. The magnetization may be acquired at the time of formation of the rock or at a later stage. In sedimentary rocks possible types of remanence are a.) Depositional Remanent Magnetization, DRM, or Post-Depositional Remanent Magnetization, PDRM, b.) Chemical Remanent Magnetization, CRM, c.) The result from the Tiki Formation is therefore interpreted as a primary magnetization. 6.6 The Parsora Formation 114. The pole positions derived from the characteristic directional components observed upon thermal demagnetization and chemical demagnetization, for the Parsora Formation of Rhaetic age are shown both before and after bedding correction (Fig.s 6.1a,b; JPA, JPB, JPC, JPD). Outcrops of Paleogene rocks from this foreland (Fig. 1A) are present in thrust sheets in the north, and in autochthonous strata bounded by orogenic belts of the Iberian Range in the south and southwest and the Catalan Coastal Ranges in the southeast. The southeastern Pyrenean foreland basin (Bentham et al., 1992; Vergés et al., 1998) corresponds to the eastern side of the Ebro foreland basin de- veloped mainly on pre-Mesozoic basement that forms an irregular triangu- lar shape bounded by the Pyrenees to the north and the Catalan Coastal Ranges to the southeast. The sections sampled for magnetic polarity rever- sal studies are located at the eastern side of the southeastern Pyrenean fore- land basin (Figs. 1B and 2). Outcrops of Paleogene rocks from this foreland (Fig. 1A) are present in thrust sheets in the north, and in autochthonous strata bounded by orogenic belts of the Iberian Range in the south and southwest and the Catalan Coastal Ranges in the southeast. The southeastern Pyrenean foreland basin (Bentham et al., 1992; Vergés et al., 1998) corresponds to the eastern side of the Ebro foreland basin de- veloped mainly on pre-Mesozoic basement that forms an irregular triangu- lar shape bounded by the Pyrenees to the north and the Catalan Coastal Ranges to the southeast. The sections sampled for magnetic polarity rever- sal studies are located at the eastern side of the southeastern Pyrenean fore- land basin (Figs. 1B and 2). The sections sampled for magnetic polarity rever- sal studies are located at the eastern side of the southeastern Pyrenean fore- land basin (Figs. 1B and 2). The sedimentary rocks that crop out in this area are Paleocene to Oligocene in age and consist of continental deposits that are below and above marine strata. These marine sediments are traditionally considered to be middle to upper Eocene in age (e.g., Hottinger, 1960; Ferrer, 1967, 1971; Reguant, 1967; Via, 1969; Serra-Kiel, 1984). The sedi- mentary formations distinguished by several authors among the marine Eocene deposits of the Vic sector of the southeastern Pyrenean foreland basin are shown schematically (Fig. 3) after the synthesis proposed in Taberner (1983). The base of the marine sequence has been interpreted as marking a rapid late Lutetian to Bartonian transgression that occurred as a result of the emplacement of the floor thrust of the Pyrenean antiformal stack (Puigdefàbregas et al., 1986). East of Vic, the basal marine strata have been dated as middle Lutetian age (Serra-Kiel, 1984). However, the first marine deposits in the southern sector of the basin were interpreted as lower-mid

diachronous and to span from middle Lutet- ian time to the base of chron C18r at 41.2 Ma (Bartonian). The top of the marine section was considered to be lower Priabonian age based on (1) nummulite species present beneath the youngest reef deposits (Serra-Kiel, 1984) and (2) the micromammal assemblage and charophyte biozonation in the continental sediments above the marine interval, that sug- gest an upper Eocene–Oligocene age (Agustí et al., 1987; Anadon et al., 1987; Feist et al., 1994). Burbank et al. (1992a) linked the top of their mag- netostratigraphic section from the Vic sector of the basin and the evaporites equivalent to the Cardona Formation to the significant sea-level fall that oc- curred at the Bartonian-Priabonian boundary (Haq et al., 1987), and gave an age of around 40 Ma for the evaporites of the Cardona Formation (located in Fig. 3). However, Vergés and Burbank (1996) and Serra-Kiel et al. (1998) linked these evaporites to the base of the Priabonian (37.2 Ma) after reeval- uation of the original magnetostratigraphic data (Burbank et al., 1992a) against the revised GPTS produced by Cande and Kent (1995). The char- acteristic remanent magnetization (ChRM) is defined as the linear segment trending toward the origin of the demagnetization diagram. For the cases in which such a segment could not be well resolved, due to low intensities or spurious magnetizations acquired upon heating, the remagnetization circles technique (Halls, 1978; McFadden and McElhinny, 1988) was used to recover the remanence direction of the highest temperature (nonresolved) component. To obtain the site mean direction per sampled stratigraphic level, Fischer (1953) statistics were used to average the ChRM directions. For sites that pre- sented both direct observations (end points determined from the linear seg- ment trending toward the origin of the demagnetization diagram) and remag- netization circles for the ChRM component, the combination method of McFadden and McElhinny (1988) was followed to calculate the mean direc- tion. Individual data are plotted in the declination and inclination logs together with the mean value and an additional quality criteria established as follows: class A for those sites that provide a minimum of two ChRM direction obser- vations; class B if at least one ChRM observation was available; and class C if only remagnetization circles could be defined. The mean declination and in- clination of the ChRM components at each site have been used to derive the latitude of the virtual geomagnetic pole (VGP). The sections sampled for magnetic polarity rever- sal studies are located at the eastern side of the southeastern Pyrenean fore- land basin (Figs. 1B and 2). The sedimentary rocks that crop out in this area are Paleocene to Oligocene in age and consist of continental deposits that are below and above marine strata. These marine sediments are traditionally considered to be middle to upper Eocene in age (e.g., Hottinger, 1960; Ferrer, 1967, 1971; Reguant, 1967; Via, 1969; Serra-Kiel, 1984). The sedi- mentary formations distinguished by several authors among the marine Eocene deposits of the Vic sector of the southeastern Pyrenean foreland basin are shown schematically (Fig. 3) after the synthesis proposed in Taberner (1983). The base of the marine sequence has been interpreted as marking a rapid late Lutetian to Bartonian transgression that occurred as a result of the emplacement of the floor thrust of the Pyrenean antiformal stack (Puigdefàbregas et al., 1986). East of Vic, the basal marine strata have been dated as middle Lutetian age (Serra-Kiel, 1984). However, the first marine deposits in the southern sector of the basin were interpreted as lower-mid

diachronous and to span from middle Lutet- ian time to the base of chron C18r at 41.2 Ma (Bartonian). The top of the marine section was considered to be lower Priabonian age based on (1) nummulite species present beneath the youngest reef deposits (Serra-Kiel, 1984) and (2) the micromammal assemblage and charophyte biozonation in the continental sediments above the marine interval, that sug- gest an upper Eocene–Oligocene age (Agustí et al., 1987; Anadon et al., 1987; Feist et al., 1994). Burbank et al. (1992a) linked the top of their mag- netostratigraphic section from the Vic sector of the basin and the evaporites equivalent to the Cardona Formation to the significant sea-level fall that oc- curred at the Bartonian-Priabonian boundary (Haq et al., 1987), and gave an age of around 40 Ma for the evaporites of the Cardona Formation (located in Fig. 3). However, Vergés and Burbank (1996) and Serra-Kiel et al. (1998) linked these evaporites to the base of the Priabonian (37.2 Ma) after reeval- uation of the original magnetostratigraphic data (Burbank et al., 1992a) against the revised GPTS produced by Cande and Kent (1995). For the cases in which such a segment could not be well resolved, due to low intensities or spurious magnetizations acquired upon heating, the remagnetization circles technique (Halls, 1978; McFadden and McElhinny, 1988) was used to recover the remanence direction of the highest temperature (nonresolved) component. To obtain the site mean direction per sampled stratigraphic level, Fischer (1953) statistics were used to average the ChRM directions. The mean declination and in- clination of the ChRM components at each site have been used to derive the latitude of the virtual geomagnetic pole (VGP). This parameter has been used as an indicator of the polarity (normal polarity for positive VGP latitudes and reverse polarity for negative VGP latitudes). The sections sampled for magnetic polarity rever- sal studies are located at the eastern side of the southeastern Pyrenean fore- land basin (Figs. 1B and 2). The sedimentary rocks that crop out in this area are Paleocene to Oligocene in age and consist of continental deposits that are below and above marine strata. These marine sediments are traditionally considered to be middle to upper Eocene in age (e.g., Hottinger, 1960; Ferrer, 1967, 1971; Reguant, 1967; Via, 1969; Serra-Kiel, 1984). The sedi- mentary formations distinguished by several authors among the marine Eocene deposits of the Vic sector of the southeastern Pyrenean foreland basin are shown schematically (Fig. 3) after the synthesis proposed in Taberner (1983). The base of the marine sequence has been interpreted as marking a rapid late Lutetian to Bartonian transgression that occurred as a result of the emplacement of the floor thrust of the Pyrenean antiformal stack (Puigdefàbregas et al., 1986). East of Vic, the basal marine strata have been dated as middle Lutetian age (Serra-Kiel, 1984). However, the first marine deposits in the southern sector of the basin were interpreted as lower-mid

diachronous and to span from middle Lutet- ian time to the base of chron C18r at 41.2 Ma (Bartonian). The top of the marine section was considered to be lower Priabonian age based on (1) nummulite species present beneath the youngest reef deposits (Serra-Kiel, 1984) and (2) the micromammal assemblage and charophyte biozonation in the continental sediments above the marine interval, that sug- gest an upper Eocene–Oligocene age (Agustí et al., 1987; Anadon et al., 1987; Feist et al., 1994). Burbank et al. (1992a) linked the top of their mag- netostratigraphic section from the Vic sector of the basin and the evaporites equivalent to the Cardona Formation to the significant sea-level fall that oc- curred at the Bartonian-Priabonian boundary (Haq et al., 1987), and gave an age of around 40 Ma for the evaporites of the Cardona Formation (located in Fig. 3). However, Vergés and Burbank (1996) and Serra-Kiel et al. (1998) linked these evaporites to the base of the Priabonian (37.2 Ma) after reeval- uation of the original magnetostratigraphic data (Burbank et al., 1992a) against the revised GPTS produced by Cande and Kent (1995). A low-temperature component (L) is unblocked between 150 and 300 °C and a high-temperature component (H) is unblocked usually above 300 °C until temperatures of about 450–500 °C. Component L has always a northerly declination and moderate to steep downward inclination (~60°) before rotation of bedding to the horizontal. The mean direction before tectonic correction for component L corresponds to the geocentric dipole direction for the present latitude of the sections and therefore can be related to a secondary recent overprint. Typical examples of thermal demagnetization are illustrated in Figures 4, 5, and 6. A multicomponent character of the NRM is clearly shown in the majority of cases. In some instances (Figs. 4C and 5, A and C) samples show a spurious behavior at low temperatures, precluding the determination of a well-defined ChRM. These events include development of the San Andreas–San Jacinto fault system and uplift of the Transverse Ranges. The badlands sequence also spans three of the four most recent North American Land Mammal “ages” and therefore coincides with important trans-Beringian and Neotropical mammal dispersal events. No other terrestrial sequence in North Amer- ica records relatively continuous deposition over this interval of time. In this report, it was determined that the age of the Shutt Ranch assemblage is between 0.99 and 0.78 Ma. If estimates for the time of deposition of strata overlying the Shutt Ranch local- ity are accurate, then deposition in this part of the Badlands did not cease un- til ca. 0.8 to 0.5 Ma. Thus, the shift in the Badlands from an aggradational sys- tem to one of erosion and degradation is constrained to a time postdating about 0.8 Ma. At BGC, only thermal demagnetization techniques were performed. After measuring the intensity and direction of the natural remanent magnetization (NRM) of all samples, each was subsequently demagnetized by stepwise heating at 40 °C intervals starting at 120 and ending at 680 °C. In order to determine the dominant magnetic mineral, Hehn et al. (1996) subjected 15 samples from the Eden Hot Springs–Jack Rabbit Trail section to isothermal remanent magnetization (IRM) analysis. Of these, 13 showed sat- uration magnetization behavior indicative of magnetite as the dominant car- rier, whereas two samples showed behavior suggestive of hematite. Behavior during thermal demagnetization showed the removal of a low-temperature overprint component, possibly due to goethite, by 200 °C. At successively higher temperatures, consistent magnetization directions were generally ob- tained to about 560 °C, above which decreases in intensity and unpredictable changes in direction occurred. This supports the conclusion that magnetite was the primary carrier of the characteristic remanent magnetization (ChRM), given a Curie temperature for that mineral of about 580 °C. However, when the normal and reversed polarity data are analyzed sepa- rately for each group, sites of normal polarity appear to be deflected coun- terclockwise to a greater degree than sites of reversed polarity, although in the Landfill–El Casco section the opposite is observed. This paper details the development of that framework by using paleo- magnetic and mammalian biochronological data. It modifies and expands upon the magnetostratigraphic foundation developed in Hehn et al. (1996) for the lower part of the Badlands section and presents new mag- neto-biostratigraphic data for the upper part. The new framework is then used to reexamine, and refine where necessary, the timing of local tec- tonic and sedimentological events recorded within the sequence. There are 22 major reversal boundaries in the global magnetic polarity time scale (MPTS) over the ~6 m.y. represented by the Badlands sequence, thus allowing a potential geologic resolution at a scale of about 0.27 m.y. This paper also reexamines the counterclockwise tectonic rotation of the Badlands region reported in Hehn et al. (1996). It briefly attempts to resolve the discrepancy between the paleomagnetic data and previous models based on seismic studies that predict clockwise vertical axis rotation in this region. B6, PAGES 12,853-12,863, JUNE 10, 1999 Paleomagnetism of an east-west transect across the Cascade arc in southern Washington: Implications for regional tectonism Jonathan T. Hagstrum U.S. Geological Survey, Menlo Park, California Donald A. Swanson U.S. Geological Survey, Hawaiian Volcano Observatory, Hawaii National Park Russell C. Evarts U.S. Geological Survey, Menlo Park, California Abstract. Paleomagnetic data from a transect across the Cascade arc in southern Washington were collected to test models of vertical axis rotations for this part of the Pacific Northwest and to provide information on the tectonic history of the St. Helens seismic zone. The 75 site-mean directions are divided into three groups based on isotopic, fission track, and stratigraphic ages. Group 1 consists of samples from rocks deposited between 39 and 30 Ma and shows a mean clockwise vertical axis rotation of 34 ø + 13 ø, group 2 consists of samples from rocks deposited be- tween 30 and 24 Ma and shows a mean clockwise rotation of 17 ø + 11 o, and group 3 consists of samples from rocks between 24 and 16 Ma and shows a mean clockwise rotation of 20 ø + 12 ø. Al- though these three values of rotation are statistically indistinguishable at the 95% confid

eismic zone (SHZ). The available paleomagnetic data for Eocene-Oligocene rocks west of the seismic zone show clockwise vertical axis rotations of 30 ø + 8 ø and 35 ø + 9 ø consistent with the value for group 1. The rotational values for groups 2 and 3 and the intrusive suite of Kidd Creek (13 Ma), despite their different ages, have similar values east of the SHZ. Comparing these groups of data east and west of the seismic zone indicates a differential rotation of 10 ø + 3 ø across it. In addition, the rates of rotation in southern Washington are similar to those for rocks in the western Cascades of Oregon and indicate that rotational deformation of Miocene age extends northward into southern Washington and eastward into the axis of the arc. 1. Introduction Paleomagnetic studies of Cenozoic rocks in the Pacific Northwest have been instrumental in documenting clockwise vertical axis rotations of crustal blocks within the convergent continental margin [Simpson and Cox, 1977; Beck, 1980; Wells et al., 1984]. Distributed results from the forearc, arc, and back arc regions have indicated that rotations tend to in- crease with age and proximity to the coast [Wells and Heller, 1988; Wells et al., 1989], apparently resulting from dextral shear caused by oblique subduction of the J

from the forearc, arc, and back arc regions have indicated that rotations tend to in- crease with age and proximity to the coast [Wells and Heller, 1988; Wells et al., 1989], apparently resulting from dextral shear caused by oblique subduction of the Juan de Fuca plate [Beck, 1980; England and Wells, 1991]. Rotations have been accommodated within the upper crust of the arc and forearc re- gions by motion along intermediate-scale and smaller strike- slip faults [Wells and Coe, 1985]. B6, PAGES 12,853-12,863, JUNE 10, 1999 Paleomagnetism of an east-west transect across the Cascade arc in southern Washington: Implications for regional tectonism Jonathan T. Hagstrum U.S. Geological Survey, Menlo Park, California Donald A. Swanson U.S. Geological Survey, Hawaiian Volcano Observatory, Hawaii National Park Russell C. Evarts U.S. Geological Survey, Menlo Park, California Abstract. Paleomagnetic data from a transect across the Cascade arc in southern Washington were collected to test models of vertical axis rotations for this part of the Pacific Northwest and to provide information on the tectonic history of the St. Helens seismic zone. The 75 site-mean directions are divided into three groups based on isotopic, fission track, and stratigraphic ages. Group 1 consists of samples from rocks deposited between 39 and 30 Ma and shows a mean clockwise vertical axis rotation of 34 ø + 13 ø, group 2 consists of samples from rocks deposited be- tween 30 and 24 Ma and shows a mean clockwise rotation of 17 ø + 11 o, and group 3 consists of samples from rocks between 24 and 16 Ma and shows a mean clockwise rotation of 20 ø + 12 ø. Al- though these three values of rotation are statistically indistinguishable at the 95% confid

eismic zone (SHZ). The available paleomagnetic data for Eocene-Oligocene rocks west of the seismic zone show clockwise vertical axis rotations of 30 ø + 8 ø and 35 ø + 9 ø consistent with the value for group 1. The rotational values for groups 2 and 3 and the intrusive suite of Kidd Creek (13 Ma), despite their different ages, have similar values east of the SHZ. Comparing these groups of data east and west of the seismic zone indicates a differential rotation of 10 ø + 3 ø across it. In addition, the rates of rotation in southern Washington are similar to those for rocks in the western Cascades of Oregon and indicate that rotational deformation of Miocene age extends northward into southern Washington and eastward into the axis of the arc. 1. Introduction Paleomagnetic studies of Cenozoic rocks in the Pacific Northwest have been instrumental in documenting clockwise vertical axis rotations of crustal blocks within the convergent continental margin [Simpson and Cox, 1977; Beck, 1980; Wells et al., 1984]. Distributed results from the forearc, arc, and back arc regions have indicated that rotations tend to in- crease with age and proximity to the coast [Wells and Heller, 1988; Wells et al., 1989], apparently resulting from dextral shear caused by oblique subduction of the J

from the forearc, arc, and back arc regions have indicated that rotations tend to in- crease with age and proximity to the coast [Wells and Heller, 1988; Wells et al., 1989], apparently resulting from dextral shear caused by oblique subduction of the Juan de Fuca plate [Beck, 1980; England and Wells, 1991]. Rotations have been accommodated within the upper crust of the arc and forearc re- gions by motion along intermediate-scale and smaller strike- slip faults [Wells and Coe, 1985]. Hagstrum U.S. Geological Survey, Menlo Park, California Donald A. Swanson U.S. Geological Survey, Hawaiian Volcano Observatory, Hawaii National Park Russell C. Evarts U.S. Geological Survey, Menlo Park, California Abstract. Paleomagnetic data from a transect across the Cascade arc in southern Washington were collected to test models of vertical axis rotations for this part of the Pacific Northwest and to provide information on the tectonic history of the St. Helens seismic zone. The 75 site-mean directions are divided into three groups based on isotopic, fission track, and stratigraphic ages. Group 1 consists of samples from rocks deposited between 39 and 30 Ma and shows a mean clockwise vertical axis rotation of 34 ø + 13 ø, group 2 consists of samples from rocks deposited be- tween 30 and 24 Ma and shows a mean clockwise rotation of 17 ø + 11 o, and group 3 consists of samples from rocks between 24 and 16 Ma and shows a mean clockwise rotation of 20 ø + 12 ø. Al- though these three values of rotation are statistically indistinguishable at the 95% confid

eismic zone (SHZ). The available paleomagnetic data for Eocene-Oligocene rocks west of the seismic zone show clockwise vertical axis rotations of 30 ø + 8 ø and 35 ø + 9 ø consistent with the value for group 1. The rotational values for groups 2 and 3 and the intrusive suite of Kidd Creek (13 Ma), despite their different ages, have similar values east of the SHZ. Comparing these groups of data east and west of the seismic zone indicates a differential rotation of 10 ø + 3 ø across it. In addition, the rates of rotation in southern Washington are similar to those for rocks in the western Cascades of Oregon and indicate that rotational deformation of Miocene age extends northward into southern Washington and eastward into the axis of the arc. 1. Rotations have been accommodated within the upper crust of the arc and forearc re- gions by motion along intermediate-scale and smaller strike- slip faults [Wells and Coe, 1985]. Specimens from the area along the Atera fault show unblocking temperature less than 350øC for the low-temperature component magnetization, whereas the low-temperature component magnetization of many localities from the peripheral area of the Nohi Rhyolite has higher unblocking temperature about 500øC. sion, latest Creta- ceous to Paleocene volcanic activity yielded the Kasagatake Rhyolites and Oamamiyama Group. These rhyolites and group are composed chiefly of many sheets of welded pyroclastics. The Late Cretaceous to Paleogene igneous activity is divided into five stages, I to V in ascending stratigraphic order [Harayama et al., 1985]. The Nohi Rhyolite was formed during stages I to III, whereas the Kasagatake Rhyolites and Oamamiyama Group are restricted to stage III. A new model is developed to explain the tectonic rotation. of SW Japan. The curvature of the Median Tectonic Line (MTL) is a clue to the higher-order approximation of the tectonics for SW Japan (Figure 1). Analysis of Paleomagnetic Results The analysis of the paleomagnetic data illus- trates well the difficulties in obtaining reliable re- sults from shallow-water carbonates and diamic- tites. Remanence directions from the carbonates of the Trezona and Nuccaleena Formations are widely scattered and poorly defined. Their rela- tively low unblocking temperatures (<600 °C) and isothermal remanent magnetization (IRM) tests of the magnetic mineralogy in these forma- tions (method of Lowrie, 1990) suggest that mag- netite and goethite are the principal remanence carriers. The scattering and poor definition of the magnetization directions, as well as the common presence of goethite, suggest that the carbonates carry unstable magnetizations unsuitable for use in paleomagnetic studies. Thus, the carbonates have not been included in subsequent analysis. The Yaltipena and Elatina Formations yielded much better results overall. d during the Ter- tiary uplift of the Flinders Ranges (Wellman and Greenhalgh, 1988). In both the Yaltipena and Elatina samples, the site mean C component directions have moder- ate to shallow inclinations and either north- northwest or southwest declinations (Fig. 6), al- though there are slight differences in the distribution of the site mean directions from section to section (see Table 1 for summary of data). The paleomagnetic results from the Elatina Formation of the central Flinders Ranges yield the first positive regional- scale fold test (significant at the 99% level), as well as at least three magnetic polarity inter- vals. Stratigraphic discontinuities typical of glacial successions prevent the application of a magnetic polarity stratigraphy to regional cor- relation, but the positive fold test and multiple reversals confirm the previous low paleolati- tude interpretation of these rocks (mean D = 214.9°, I = –14.7°,a 95 = 12.7°, paleolatitude = 7.5°). Although the pres- ence of cap carbonates like the Nuccaleena have been interpreted in the past as a return to warm tropical conditions (e.g., Lemon and Gostin, 1990), the proposed unusual geochemical condi- tions associated with these carbonates as well as their subtidal depositional settings (Kennedy, 1996; Hoffman et al., 1998) make the determina- tion of temperate vs. tropical depositional environ- ments for the cap carbonates difficult at present. The Elatina and Nuccaleena Formations were sampled along three sections that afforded the best opportunities to conduct a fold test (see Figs. 1A and 3). Two of these sections, the Bennett Spring section (31°13¢S lat, 138°48¢E long) and the Trezona Bore section (31°17¢S lat, 138°39¢E long) are ~18 km apart and are on opposite sides of a salt diapir. The third section at Warcowie (31°47¢S lat, 138°40¢E long) is located ~55 km south-southeast of Trezona Bore. The average bedding attitude of the Elatina and Nuccaleena Formations at the Bennett Spring Section is strike 165°, dip 14°NE; at the Trezona Bore section, strike 170°, dip 16°SW; and at Warcowie, strike 055°, dip 85°NW. Stability Tests To help determine whether the site mean C component data from the central Flinders Ranges represent a primary magnetic remanence (i.e., a detrital or an early diagenetic remanence) or some later magnetization, we applied geological or field stability tests to the central Flinders data to link the magnetizations to the geologic history of the rocks. Four tests commonly used for sedi- mentary rocks are the fold test, the reversals test, the conglomerate test, and the unconformity test (see review in Butler, 1992). Stratigraphic discontinuities typical of glacial successions prevent the application of a magnetic polarity stratigraphy to regional cor- relation, but the positive fold test and multiple reversals confirm the previous low paleolati- tude interpretation of these rocks (mean D = 214.9°, I = –14.7°,a 95 = 12.7°, paleolatitude = 7.5°). The underlying preglacial Yaltipena For- mation also carries low magnetic inclinations (mean D = 204.0°, I = –16.4°,a 95 = 11.0°, paleo- latitude = 8.4°), suggesting that Australia was located at low paleolatitude at the onset of glaciation. The number of magnetic polarity in- tervals present within the Elatina Formation and the Elatina’s lithostratigraphic relation- ship to other Marinoan glacial deposits suggest that glaciation persisted at low latitudes in Aus- tralia for a minimum of several hundreds of thousands to millions of years. Stratigraphic discontinuities typical of glacial successions prevent the application of a magnetic polarity stratigraphy to regional cor- relation, but the positive fold test and multiple reversals confirm the previous low paleolati- tude interpretation of these rocks (mean D = 214.9°, I = –14.7°,a 95 = 12.7°, paleolatitude = 7.5°). Received 1998 November 22; in original form 1997 July 22 SUMMARY The palaeomagnetic data that are available for the eastern Fennoscandian Shield are too sparse to allow any palaeomagnetic constraints to be determined for intracratonic horizontal movements in this part of the shield. To address this issue we have obtained new palaeomagnetic data from maﬁc and ultramaﬁc plutons, sills, dykes and basement country rocks in the Kola, Belomorian and Karelian provinces of the Fennoscandian Shield. A number of natural remanent magnetization (NRM) components were isolated, and we associate these with various events of Precambrian tectonomagmatic activity within the eastern Fennoscandian Shield. 36 palaeomagnetic poles were obtained. 12 poles, with ages ranging from 1700 Ma to 2450 Ma, satisfy the accepted reliability criteria (corresponding to the ‘B-category’ of Briden & DuV 1981). Received 1998 November 22; in original form 1997 July 22 SUMMARY The palaeomagnetic data that are available for the eastern Fennoscandian Shield are too sparse to allow any palaeomagnetic constraints to be determined for intracratonic horizontal movements in this part of the shield. To address this issue we have obtained new palaeomagnetic data from maﬁc and ultramaﬁc plutons, sills, dykes and basement country rocks in the Kola, Belomorian and Karelian provinces of the Fennoscandian Shield. A number of natural remanent magnetization (NRM) components were isolated, and we associate these with various events of Precambrian tectonomagmatic activity within the eastern Fennoscandian Shield. 36 palaeomagnetic poles were obtained. 12 poles, with ages ranging from 1700 Ma to 2450 Ma, satisfy the accepted reliability criteria (corresponding to the ‘B-category’ of Briden & DuV 1981). For the Karelian Province, reference poles are presented for the Burakovka gabbro-norites (19.5 ° S, 262.6° E, A95=7.2° ; Sm–Nd age of 2439± 22 Ma), the Matozero doleritic dykes (20.6° S, 308.5° E, A95=12.3° ; U–Pb age of 2150 ± 60 Ma), and the Ropruchey Sill gabbro- dolerites (40.5 ° N, 229.8° E, A95=8.1° ; U–Pb age of 1770 ± 12 Ma). Although some NRM components of other rocks are not as precisely dated, a number of palaeomagnetic poles are in good internal agreement, forming two tracks of the Lower Proterozoic apparent polar wander path (APWP). A preliminary version of the pre-Svecofennian APWP tracks for the Karelian and Kola–Belomorian provinces is proposed. Our results conﬁrm the general drift pattern of Fennoscandia in the Proterozoic and support the idea of the absence of large-scale block movements within t

gnetic evidence that can resolve that degree of movement. An apparent polar wander path (APWP) for the Fennoscandian Shield has recently been constructed for the time interval 2850–600 Ma, under the assumption that the Shield remained tectonically coherent during this time (Elming et al . 1993). There is, however, geological evidence which indicates that signiﬁcant intracratonic occurred during this time. Gorbatschev & Bogdanova (1993) provided evidence for rifting and the possible break-up of the shield between 2500 and 2000 Ma. The resultant basins were then closed due to a collisional orogeny between 1950 and 1820 Ma, possibly marking the formation of a Proterozoic supercontinent (Piper 1987). On the other hand, the Archaean and Palaeoproterozoic palaeomagnetic data from the Fennoscandian Shield were predominantly obtained from the Karelian and Svecofennian provinces. Few poles from the Lapland granulite belt of the Belomorian Province and from Kola Province were available for the Elming et al. (1993) compilation and their reconstruction of the Fennoscandian APWP. Received 1998 November 22; in original form 1997 July 22 SUMMARY The palaeomagnetic data that are available for the eastern Fennoscandian Shield are too sparse to allow any palaeomagnetic constraints to be determined for intracratonic horizontal movements in this part of the shield. To address this issue we have obtained new palaeomagnetic data from maﬁc and ultramaﬁc plutons, sills, dykes and basement country rocks in the Kola, Belomorian and Karelian provinces of the Fennoscandian Shield. A number of natural remanent magnetization (NRM) components were isolated, and we associate these with various events of Precambrian tectonomagmatic activity within the eastern Fennoscandian Shield. 36 palaeomagnetic poles were obtained. 12 poles, with ages ranging from 1700 Ma to 2450 Ma, satisfy the accepted reliability criteria (corresponding to the ‘B-category’ of Briden & DuV 1981). An apparent polar wander path (APWP) for the Fennoscandian Shield has recently been constructed for the time interval 2850–600 Ma, under the assumption that the Shield remained tectonically coherent during this time (Elming et al . 1993). There is, however, geological evidence which indicates that signiﬁcant intracratonic occurred during this time. Gorbatschev & Bogdanova (1993) provided evidence for rifting and the possible break-up of the shield between 2500 and 2000 Ma. To address this issue we have obtained new palaeomagnetic data from maﬁc and ultramaﬁc plutons, sills, dykes and basement country rocks in the Kola, Belomorian and Karelian provinces of the Fennoscandian Shield. A number of natural remanent magnetization (NRM) components were isolated, and we associate these with various events of Precambrian tectonomagmatic activity within the eastern Fennoscandian Shield. 36 palaeomagnetic poles were obtained. 12 poles, with ages ranging from 1700 Ma to 2450 Ma, satisfy the accepted reliability criteria (corresponding to the ‘B-category’ of Briden & DuV 1981). Received 1998 November 22; in original form 1997 July 22 SUMMARY The palaeomagnetic data that are available for the eastern Fennoscandian Shield are too sparse to allow any palaeomagnetic constraints to be determined for intracratonic horizontal movements in this part of the shield. To address this issue we have obtained new palaeomagnetic data from maﬁc and ultramaﬁc plutons, sills, dykes and basement country rocks in the Kola, Belomorian and Karelian provinces of the Fennoscandian Shield. A number of natural remanent magnetization (NRM) components were isolated, and we associate these with various events of Precambrian tectonomagmatic activity within the eastern Fennoscandian Shield. 36 palaeomagnetic poles were obtained. 12 poles, with ages ranging from 1700 Ma to 2450 Ma, satisfy the accepted reliability criteria (corresponding to the ‘B-category’ of Briden & DuV 1981). Of these, six might be classiﬁed as reference poles. For the Kola and Belomorian provinces there are poles from the Main Range gabbro-dolerites (16.7° S,

For the Karelian Province, reference poles are presented for the Burakovka gabbro-norites (19.5 ° S, 262.6° E, A95=7.2° ; Sm–Nd age of 2439± 22 Ma), the Matozero doleritic dykes (20.6° S, 308.5° E, A95=12.3° ; U–Pb age of 2150 ± 60 Ma), and the Ropruchey Sill gabbro- dolerites (40.5 ° N, 229.8° E, A95=8.1° ; U–Pb age of 1770 ± 12 Ma). An apparent polar wander path (APWP) for the Fennoscandian Shield has recently been constructed for the time interval 2850–600 Ma, under the assumption that the Shield remained tectonically coherent during this time (Elming et al . 1993). There is, however, geological evidence which indicates that signiﬁcant intracratonic occurred during this time. Gorbatschev & Bogdanova (1993) provided evidence for rifting and the possible break-up of the shield between 2500 and 2000 Ma. The resultant basins were then closed due to a collisional orogeny between 1950 and 1820 Ma, possibly marking the formation of a Proterozoic supercontinent (Piper 1987). On the other hand, the Archaean and Palaeoproterozoic palaeomagnetic data from the Fennoscandian Shield were predominantly obtained from the Karelian and Svecofennian provinces. Few poles from the Lapland granulite belt of the Belomorian Province and from Kola Province were available for the Elming et al. (1993) compilation and their reconstruction of the Fennoscandian APWP. The Monchegorsk ultramaﬁc layered pluton is situated in the central part of the Kola Peninsula, to the north of the Pechenga–Varzuga Tectonic Zone (Fig. 1). It is made up of two limbs (Fig. 2). The northwestern limb consists mainly of ultramaﬁc rocks (dunites, harzburgites and pyroxenites), whereas the eastern limb exposes maﬁc-ultramaﬁc rocks of the upper part of the intrusion (Balashov et al . 1993). n good internal agreement, forming two tracks of the Lower Proterozoic apparent polar wander path (APWP). A preliminary version of the pre-Svecofennian APWP tracks for the Karelian and Kola–Belomorian provinces is proposed. Our results conﬁrm the general drift pattern of Fennoscandia in the Proterozoic and support the idea of the absence of large-scale block movements within the Fennoscandian Shield since Jatulian times (2300–2100 Ma). To help constrain the relative positions of the various tectonic blocks of the eastern Fennoscandian Shield during pre-Jatulian times, more new palaeomagnetic and radiometric data need to be added to the available palaeomagnetic database. Palaeomagnetic data oVer the possibility of addressing some of these questions; until now, however, only the Canadian Shield has yielded enough Precambrian palaeomagnetic data to indi- cate signiﬁcant intracratonic movements (Symons 1991). As for the Fennoscandian Shield, there is as yet no palaeomagnetic evidence that can resolve that degree of movement. An apparent polar wander path (APWP) for the Fennoscandian Shield has recently been constructed for the time interval 2850–600 Ma, under the assumption that the Shield remained tectonically coherent during this time (Elming et al . 1993). There is, however, geological evidence which indicates that signiﬁcant intracratonic occurred during this time. Gorbatschev & Bogdanova (1993) provided evidence for rifting and the possible break-up of the shield between 2500 and 2000 Ma. The resultant basins were then closed due to a collisional orogeny between 1950 and 1820 Ma, possibly marking the formation of a Proterozoic supercontinent (Piper 1987). On the other hand, the Arc

The resultant basins were then closed due to a collisional orogeny between 1950 and 1820 Ma, possibly marking the formation of a Proterozoic supercontinent (Piper 1987). Although some NRM components of other rocks are not as precisely dated, a number of palaeomagnetic poles are in good internal agreement, forming two tracks of the Lower Proterozoic apparent polar wander path (APWP). A preliminary version of the pre-Svecofennian APWP tracks for the Karelian and Kola–Belomorian provinces is proposed. Our results conﬁrm the general drift pattern of Fennoscandia in the Proterozoic and support the idea of the absence of large-scale block movements within t

gnetic evidence that can resolve that degree of movement. An apparent polar wander path (APWP) for the Fennoscandian Shield has recently been constructed for the time interval 2850–600 Ma, under the assumption that the Shield remained tectonically coherent during this time (Elming et al . 1993). There is, however, geological evidence which indicates that signiﬁcant intracratonic occurred during this time. Gorbatschev & Bogdanova (1993) provided evidence for rifting and the possible break-up of the shield between 2500 and 2000 Ma. The resultant basins were then closed due to a collisional orogeny between 1950 and 1820 Ma, possibly marking the formation of a Proterozoic supercontinent (Piper 1987). On the other hand, the Archaean and Palaeoproterozoic palaeomagnetic data from the Fennoscandian Shield were predominantly obtained from the Karelian and Svecofennian provinces. Few poles from the Lapland granulite belt of the Belomorian Province and from Kola Province were available for the Elming et al. (1993) compilation and their reconstruction of the Fennoscandian APWP. To address this issue we have obtained new palaeomagnetic data from maﬁc and ultramaﬁc plutons, sills, dykes and basement country rocks in the Kola, Belomorian and Karelian provinces of the Fennoscandian Shield. Received 1998 November 22; in original form 1997 July 22 SUMMARY The palaeomagnetic data that are available for the eastern Fennoscandian Shield are too sparse to allow any palaeomagnetic constraints to be determined for intracratonic horizontal movements in this part of the shield. To address this issue we have obtained new palaeomagnetic data from maﬁc and ultramaﬁc plutons, sills, dykes and basement country rocks in the Kola, Belomorian and Karelian provinces of the Fennoscandian Shield. A number of natural remanent magnetization (NRM) components were isolated, and we associate these with various events of Precambrian tectonomagmatic activity within the eastern Fennoscandian Shield. 36 palaeomagnetic poles were obtained. 12 poles, with ages ranging from 1700 Ma to 2450 Ma, satisfy the accepted reliability criteria (corresponding to the ‘B-category’ of Briden & DuV 1981). Of these, six might be classiﬁed as reference poles. For the Kola and Belomorian provinces there are poles from the Main Range gabbro-dolerites (16.7° S,

gnetic evidence that can resolve that degree of movement. An apparent polar wander path (APWP) for the Fennoscandian Shield has recently been constructed for the time interval 2850–600 Ma, under the assumption that the Shield remained tectonically coherent during this time (Elming et al . 1993). There is, however, geological evidence which indicates that signiﬁcant intracratonic occurred during this time. Gorbatschev & Bogdanova (1993) provided evidence for rifting and the possible break-up of the shield between 2500 and 2000 Ma. The resultant basins were then closed due to a collisional orogeny between 1950 and 1820 Ma, possibly marking the formation of a Proterozoic supercontinent (Piper 1987). On the other hand, the Archaean and Palaeoproterozoic palaeomagnetic data from the Fennoscandian Shield were predominantly obtained from the Karelian and Svecofennian provinces. Few poles from the Lapland granulite belt of the Belomorian Province and from Kola Province were available for the Elming et al. (1993) compilation and their reconstruction of the Fennoscandian APWP. An apparent polar wander path (APWP) for the Fennoscandian Shield has recently been constructed for the time interval 2850–600 Ma, under the assumption that the Shield remained tectonically coherent during this time (Elming et al . 1993). There is, however, geological evidence which indicates that signiﬁcant intracratonic occurred during this time. Gorbatschev & Bogdanova (1993) provided evidence for rifting and the possible break-up of the shield between 2500 and 2000 Ma. CONCLUSIONS Demagnetisation data from rocks of the Karoo Super- group are generally of poor quality. The best indivi- dual demagnetisation data are observed from the Middle-Jurassic lsalo Group, but poor remanence grouping precludes calculation of a group mean direction. Directional results from the Late Permian- Early Jurassic Sakamena and the Late Carboni- ferous(?)-Early Permian Sakoa Group show gross similarities with earlier published data. Most data, however, are of relatively poor quality and there is no firm evidence that proves a primary remanence. Local fold and conglomerate tests were inconclusive due to the poor magnetic properties of the rocks. A comparison with West Gondwana palaeomag- netic poles shows that the Lottes and Rowley (19901 fit produces the best palaeomagnetic match between Madagascar and East Africa (Somalia), but other less tight fits, can be considered within the resolution of the palasomagnetic data, most notably for’llpper Permian-Lower Triassic times (e.g. Coffin and Rabino- witz, 1987). CONCLUSIONS Demagnetisation data from rocks of the Karoo Super- group are generally of poor quality. The best indivi- dual demagnetisation data are observed from the Middle-Jurassic lsalo Group, but poor remanence grouping precludes calculation of a group mean direction. Directional results from the Late Permian- Early Jurassic Sakamena and the Late Carboni- ferous(?)-Early Permian Sakoa Group show gross similarities with earlier published data. Most data, however, are of relatively poor quality and there is no firm evidence that proves a primary remanence. Local fold and conglomerate tests were inconclusive due to the poor magnetic properties of the rocks. A dual-polarity characteristic remanent magnetization (ChRM) resolved from most samples by thermal demagnetization is shown to have been acquired prior to folding. The primary nature of the ChRM is corroborated by the discovery of the same magnetic polarity at equivalent stratigraphic levels in more than one section. A dual-polarity characteristic remanent magnetization (ChRM) resolved from most samples by thermal demagnetization is shown to have been acquired prior to folding. The primary nature of the ChRM is corroborated by the discovery of the same magnetic polarity at equivalent stratigraphic levels in more than one section. A dual-polarity characteristic remanent magnetization (ChRM) resolved from most samples by thermal demagnetization is shown to have been acquired prior to folding. The primary nature of the ChRM is corroborated by the discovery of the same magnetic polarity at equivalent stratigraphic levels in more than one section. The relative sample VGP (virtual geomagnetic pole) latitudes deﬁne nine magnetozones for the three major constituent members of the formation. Comparison with the Mid-Triassic magnetic polarity sequence observed from the western Tethyan region appears to indicate that the bulk of the Badong Formation is Anisian in age and that Ladinian sediments are largely missing. Geology During Pliocene and Pleistocene time ( V2.4^ 0.8 Ma), Afar was covered by a thick sequence of £ood basalts, referred to as the Afar Stratoid Series (mean age 1.7 þ 0.2 Ma; Fig. 2) [2,14^17]. Subsequent faulting has produced a landscape dominated by horsts and grabens and faults and ¢ssures, which have a dominant northwest^south- east orientation. In addition, several of the lava flows record intriguing geomagnetic field behavior associated with polarity transitions, excursions, or large secular variation events. Interestingly, the transitional or anomalous virtual geomagnetic poles (VGPs) tend to cluster in two nearly antipodal regions, one in the northern Pacific Ocean and the other in the southwest Indian Ocean. One lava flow has recorded both of the antipodal transitional components, with the two components residing in magnetic minerals with unblocking temperatures above and below V500‡C, respectively. Reheating and partial remagnetization by the overlying flow cannot explain either of the transitional directions because both differ significantly from that of the reversely magnetized overlying flow. The high-temperature component gives a VGP in the northern Pacific, whereas the lower-temperature component gives a nearly antipodal VGP south of Cape Town, South Africa. Hence, the configuration of the geomagnetic field appears to have jumped nearly instantaneously from a northern-hemisphere transitional state to a southern-hemisphere one during this normal- to-reverse polarity transition. ß 2000 Elsevier

Magnetizations of the specimens were measured in a 2G Enterprises cryogenic magnetometer (model 760R with AC SQUIDs) with an automated sample handler and an in-line alternating ¢eld (AF) unit, all of which reside in a magnetically shielded room. All specimens were progressively demagnetized using standard AF or thermal methods. carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: Thus, propagation and localization in central Afar have not had the same influence in causing crustal block rotations or, perhaps more likely, have not reached the same stage of evolution as seen in eastern Afar. In addition, several of the lava flows record intriguing geomagnetic field behavior associated with polarity transitions, excursions, or large secular variation events. Interestingly, the transitional or anomalous virtual geomagnetic poles (VGPs) tend to cluster in two nearly antipodal regions, one in the northern Pacific Ocean and the other in the southwest Indian Ocean. One lava flow has recorded both of the antipodal transitional components, with the two components residing in magnetic minerals with unblocking temperatures above and below V500‡C, respectively. Reheating and partial remagnetization by the overlying flow cannot explain either of the transitional directions because both differ significantly from that of the reversely magnetized overlying flow. The high-temperature component gives a VGP in the northern Pacific, whereas the lower-temperature component gives a nearly antipodal VGP south of Cape Town, South Africa. Hence, the configuration of the geomagnetic field appears to have jumped nearly instantaneously from a northern-hemisphere transitional state to a southern-hemisphere one during this normal- to-reverse polarity transition. ß 2000 Elsevier Science B.V. ast 2 myr has been characterized by widespread and intense crustal fragmentation that results from inhomogeneous extension across the region. In eastern Afar, this situation has evolved to localized extension associated with the westward propagation of the Gulf of Aden/Gulf of Tadjurah seafloor spreading system into the Asal^Ghoubbet Rift. During the gradual process of rift propagation and localization, crustal blocks in eastern Afar sustained clockwise rotations of V11‡. To better understand the processes of rift propagation and localization and how they affect the rest of Afar, we have collected and analyzed over 400 oriented paleomagnetic samples from 67 lava flows from central and southern Afar. Unlike eastern Afar, the mean paleomagnetic direction from central Afar indicates that vertical-axis rotations are statistically insignificant (3.6‡ þ 4.4‡), though small clockwise rotations ( 6 8‡) are permitted. Thus, propagation and localization in central Afar have not had the same influence in causing crustal block rotations or, perhaps more likely, have not reached the same stage of evolution as seen in eastern Afar. carrier_investigation_candidates.excerpt: 19 September 1996; accepted 19 June 1997 Abstract Regional glaciation is recorded at two stratigraphic levels in the Neoproterozoic Sinian succession of the Yangzi (South China) Block. A palaeomagnetic study is reported here of the upper sequence (~ 730-670 Ma) which contains red beds. An 'AI' component (D/I= 291/-57 °, a95 = 5.0°, Palaeopole 151.2°E, 0.2°N) is resolved at high unblocking temperatures and resides in specular haematite. A study of contemporaneous deformation structures suggests that this component was acquired at an early stage of lithification and yields a representative palaeolatitude (37 °) for the glaciation. Lower blocking temperature magnetizations referred to as 'A2' (D/I=297/--19 °, ~t95 =7.6 °, Palaeopole 171.8°E, 19.2°S) and 'A3' (D/1=319/-1 °, ct95=3.2 °, Palaeopole 169.1°E, 41.8°S) are later overprints correlating with probable Late Precambrian or Cambrian palaeofields. In other regions, the 'A' magnetizations were found to be partially or completely overprinted by a Recent field and/or a 'B' remanence (D/I=4/13°); the latter correlates with a remagnetization widely recorded elsewhere in South China and is attributed to the Mesozoic Indosinian Orogeny. 3-199 1. Introduction The last few years have seen a heightened interest in the Neoproterozoic Earth. This has come, in part, from recognition of the important and enig- matic changes in the biosphere during these times (Knoll and Walter, 1992; Dalziel et al., 1994). This interest has also prompted a re-evaluation of Neoproterozoic glaciation because glacial rocks of this age are often a part of distinctive facies associations; the diamictites frequently occur interbedded with rocks more often assigned to low latitudes such as carbonates, red beds and phos- phorites (Schemerhorn, 1974; Hambrey and Harland, 1981; Harland, 1983; Fairchild et al., 1994). Whether or not lowland ice sheets actually occu- pied latitudes much lower than Permo- Carboniferous and Quaternary ice has, however, been the subject of much recent debate (e.g. Meert and Van der Voo, 1994; Williams et al., 1995; Young, 1995). This debate has a bearing on such questions as the obliquity of the Earth during Neoproterozoic times (e.g. Williams, 1993). A recent palaeomagnetic study of ~600Ma Marinoan periglacial rocks in South Australia has established unequivocally that they were formed close to the ancient equator as defined by the axial geocentric dipole model (Schmidt and Williams, 1995).

ative amounts in these rocks. Selected samples were magnetized using a pulse magnetizer. The applied fields were increased in approximately logarithmic steps (2, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 40, 50, 80, 100, 120, 160, 200, 250, 300mT...) until a saturation IRM (SIRM) was achieved or the upper limit of the field in the magnetizer (2500 mT.) was reached. Subsequently samples were incrementally magnetized by the same process in the opposing direction until the IRM was reduced to zero. At this point, the applied field value defines the coercivity of the remanence (Her). The peak field in the pulse demagnetizer is unable to fully saturate haematite although it is adequate to identify the essential behaviour of this mineral. 3-199 1. Introduction The last few years have seen a heightened interest in the Neoproterozoic Earth. This has come, in part, from recognition of the important and enig- matic changes in the biosphere during these times (Knoll and Walter, 1992; Dalziel et al., 1994). This interest has also prompted a re-evaluation of Neoproterozoic glaciation because glacial rocks of this age are often a part of distinctive facies associations; the diamictites frequently occur interbedded with rocks more often assigned to low latitudes such as carbonates, red beds and phos- phorites (Schemerhorn, 1974; Hambrey and Harland, 1981; Harland, 1983; Fairchild et al., 1994). Whether or not lowland ice sheets actually occu- pied latitudes much lower than Permo- Carboniferous and Quaternary ice has, however, been the subject of much recent debate (e.g. Meert and Van der Voo, 1994; Williams et al., 1995; Young, 1995). This debate has a bearing on such questions as the obliquity of the Earth during Neoproterozoic times (e.g. Williams, 1993). A recent palaeomagnetic study of ~600Ma Marinoan periglacial rocks in South Australia has established unequivocally that they were formed close to the ancient equator as defined by the axial geocentric dipole model (Schmidt and Williams, 1995).

The acquisition of IRM is best described by a combination of curves of cumulative log Gaussian (CLG) functions. Curves are observed to be a combi- nation of at least two cumulative functions in the Sinian red sediments. This is illustrated in Fig. 4 using an adaptation of the method first described by Eyre (1994) in which the gradient of the acquisition curve is plotted against log of the applied field.

The only suggestion of another phase is the change in gradient of medium IRM curves between 200 and 300°C, The source of this feature cannot be positively iden- tified; possible causes are fine grained haematite near the superparamagnetic-single domain trans- ition or the transformation of goethite (formed from near surface weathering) into haematite (Fig. 5). There is no substantial evidence for a magnetiz- ing phase other than haematite in any of these rocks. We conclude that the remanence carrier is haematite with little or no magnetite. A.f. demag- netization is therefore unlikely to be effective and only thermal demagnetization was carried out. The complex paragenesis of haematite also identifies the need for caution when relating remanence to geological events; thus, haematite formation can relate to deposition, early (~ 100-500 years) dewa- tering (Tauxe and Badgley, 1984), or to much later diagenesis (Larson and Walker, 1982). 5. Bulk susceptibility was measured after each thermal de- magnetization step to detect heat-induced miner- alogical changes. Demagnetization behavior was variable, and most specimens display multicomponent NRMs. Where possible, remanence directions were deter- mined using principal component analysis (Kirsch- vink 1980) applied to colinear segments converging toward the origin. Components were considered stable when they were de®ned by at least three points on vector endpoint diagrams and had a max- imum angular deviation not exceeding 15 7. The overlapping nature of the blocking spectra meant that in some cases it was impossible to de®ne linear components, and remagnetization circles were of- ten required to recover the direction (McFadden and McElhinny 1988). As discussed earlier, there is no evidence for a tectonothermal event in the Ellsworth Mountains during the early Paleozoic that could reset the mag- netization, and from the Early-Middle Ordovician onward, the EWM formed part of a passive margin. The interpretation preferred here is that the mag- netization carried by the Liberty Hi

rocks record a re- magnetization. Positive fold tests in the Frazier Ridge and in this study indicate that any remag- netization is pre-Permo-Triassic. Furthermore, the paleolatitudes indicate that both magnetizations must date from the early Paleozoic. The available constraints lead us to prefer the interpretation that the Liberty Hills Formation carries a primary rem- anence. The similarity of the Nash Hills and Frazier Ridge poles is generally interpreted as supporting the integrity of the data sets. Not only do they have similar pole positions but they also have similar magnetic propertiesÐin both cases the remanence is held solely by a hematite carrier, and both record all sites with the same polarity. However, the Nash Hills pole is based on only 12 samples from par- tially remagnetized red calcareous siltstones of un- certain stratigraphic position. No correlative red calcareous sedimentary rocks were observed in the EWM during this study, and the age of the Nash Hills samples is therefore unknown. It is possible, therefore, that there could be a time gap between the deposition of the Frazier Ridge Formation and the Nash Hills siltstones, and the similarity of the magnetizations may indicate a regional early Pa- leozoic remagnetization event. Tomshin1 Geological Survey of Canada, 601 Booth Street, Ottawa, Ontario K1A 0E8, Canada (e-mail: rernst@nrcan.gc.ca) ABSTRACT This article reports the ®rst joint paleomagnetic and U-Pb geochronologic study of Precambrian diabase dikes in the Anabar Shield and adjacent Riphean cover of Siberia. It was undertaken to allow comparison with similar published studies in Laurentia and to test Proterozoic reconstructions of Siberia and Laurentia. An east-trending Kuonamka dike yielded a provisional U-Pb baddeleyite emplacement age of Ma and a virtual geomagnetic pole at 16 7S,1503 5 5 2217E ( , ). A paleomagnetic pole at 6 7N, 2347E ( , ) was obtained from ®ve Kuonamkad m=1 77 d p=1 07 d m=2 87 d p=1 47 dikes. An east-southeast-trending Chieress dike yielded a U-Pb baddeleyite emplacement age of Ma and a1384 5 2 virtual geomagnetic pole at 47N, 2587E ( , ). Kuonamka and Chieress

iberian Plate (Zonen- shain et al. 1990). The younger Viljuy aulacogen (®g. 2), consisting of the Viljuy (G1) and Ygyatinsky (G2) grabens, extends westward »600 km into the Siberian Plate (Zonenshain et al. 1990). Analysis of paleomagnetic data (Gurevich 1984; Pavlov and Pe- trov 1996, 1997; Smethurst et al. 1998) suggests a counterclockwise rotation of the portion of the Si- berian Plate north of the Viljuy aulacogen relative to that south of the aulacogen in the mid-Paleozoic (Wenlock-Esmian: 0.43±0.39 Ga). Smethurst et al. (1998) estimated a rotation of »207 about a rotation pole at 607N, 1007E, just west of the basin. Proterozoic diabase dikes are abundant in the main areas of exposed basement in the Siberian Plate and in Riphean and Vendian cover rocks (Ernst et al. 1996 and references therein). In an ear- lier study, those in and adjacent to the Anabar Shield were divided into 10 swarms on the basis of trend, location, composition, and K-Ar age (®g. 3; Okrugin et al. 1990). Five of these swarms occur in the general area of this study. The east-trending Kuonamka swarm (K-Ar ages of 1600±1200 Ma), the southeast-trending East Anabar swarm (K-Ar ages of ca. 1700 Ma), and the east-northeast-trending Central Anabar swarm (K-Ar ages of 1800±1400 Ma) intrude highly metamorphosed Archea

Ar age (®g. 3; Okrugin et al. 1990). Five of these swarms occur in the general area of this study. The east-trending Kuonamka swarm (K-Ar ages of 1600±1200 Ma), the southeast-trending East Anabar swarm (K-Ar ages of ca. 1700 Ma), and the east-northeast-trending Central Anabar swarm (K-Ar ages of 1800±1400 Ma) intrude highly metamorphosed Archean rocks and, occasionally, Early Riphean rocks. The Chieress swarm (K-Ar ages of ca. 1200±900 Ma) and the Ju- ken swarm (K-Ar ages of 1300±1200 Ma), both of east-southeast trend, cut Early Riphean cover rocks immediately to the east of the Anabar Shield. Sampling and Laboratory Procedure Eleven diabase dikes were sampled for paleomag- netism, and of these, eight were also sampled for U-Pb geochronology, during the course of a rafting expedition down the Bol'shaya Kuonamka River in the eastern Anabar Shield region (®g. 3). Each dike is assigned to one of the swarms described above, based on an analysis of its trend, petrographic and/ or geochemical characteristics, paleomagnetic di- rection, and U-Pb or previously published K-Ar age. 3 8 4 R. d Both hypotheses A and B indicate that Lower White Channel gravel was deposited by at least the Gauss chron (>2.58 Ma). However, the assignment of a Gauss versus Olduvai age for the Upper White Channel and Klondike gravel units is difficult on the basis of paleomagnetic data alone. A Gauss age for the Upper White Channel – Klondike gravel magnetopolarity zone is preferred for the following reasons. (1) Evidence from elsewhere in the northern Cordillera (Westgate et al. 1990; Duk-Rodkin et al. 1996; Barendregt et al. 1996), indicates that full-glacial conditions likely existed in the northern Cordillera prior to the Olduvai (>1.77 Ma). Near Fairbanks, Alaska, Gold Hill Loess deposition, result - ing from advancing glaciers in the Tanana River valley be - gan by the Mammoth subchron (ca. 3 Ma; Westgate et al. 1990). (2) Cores from the North Pacific Ocean indicate large- scale glaciation began abruptly in the Northern Hemisphere during the Gauss chron (before 2.58 Ma; Krissek 1995; Rea et al. 1995). Ma to <780 ka, including the Jaramillo subchron (1.1 Ma). ted in this paper, we have analyzed the paleomagnetism of the Siwalik Group at Tinau Khola and Surai Khola, and the Dumri Formation along Tansen road (Fig. 1). Complete results will be reported elsewhere, but we report here observations on lithologic control of paleomagnetism. Our pilot set of samples focused on three rock types: sand- stone, laminated siltstone, and paleosol (i.e., mas- sive, pedoturbated and bioturbated siltstone). Our results show that paleosols (Fig. 3, A–C) and sandstones (Fig. 3, D–F) have erratic thermal demagnetization behaviors. The few sandy silt- stones that were sampled showed more coherent behavior. In contrast, thermal demagnetization of samples from laminated siltstone (Fig. 4) dis- played coherent demagnetization trajectories, many without significant directional changes dur- ing thermal demagnetization. Our results show that wherever possible in the Siwalik Group of Nepal, laminated siltstone should be sampled for paleomagnetic studies, and we have exclusively focused the remainder of our paleomagnetic sam- pling on laminated siltstones. Drawing the dis- tinction in the field between laminated siltstone and paleosols is essential, even though paleosols have only recently been recognized in the Siwalik Group in Nepal (Harrison et al., 1993; Quade et al., 1995). Although we lack detailed petrographic and anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility information necessary for detailed comparison between the Siwalik sedi- ments of Nepal and those from Pakistan, some useful comparisons and contrasts can be made. In both regions, laminated and unaltered rocks (termed gray sediments in Pakistan) often exhibit coherent demagnetization behaviors with un- blocking temperatures extending to 680 °C and often concentrated between 600 °C and 680 °C (Fig. 4). Results of thermal demagnetization experiments on samples from the Siwalik Group in central and western Nepal demonstrate that lami- nated siltstones yield paleomagnetic data use- ful for tectonic and magnetostratigraphic studies. Sandstones and paleosols of the Siwalik Group, however, generally display highly erratic paleomagnetic behavior during thermal demagnetization. On the basis of these observations, siltstones from a well-ex- posed, 2423-m-thick section of the Siwalik Group in Khutia Khola, far western Nepal, were sampled for magnetic polarity stratig- raphy. The Siwalik Group is composed of in- formal lower, middle, and upper members. Correlation of the resulting polarity stratig- raphy with the geomagnetic polarity timescale indicates that the exposed section spans 13.30 to 7.65 Ma. The lower-middle Siwalik bound- ary occurs at 11.05 Ma, near the beginning of chron C5n. The rate of sediment accumula- tion increases upsection, similar to rate changes previously observed in the Pakistan Siwalik Group, and probably in response to increasing proximity of the Himalayan thrust belt. In the Khutia Khola section, a discordant declination indicates that this region has ro- tated about a vertical axis 16.6° counterclock- wise with respect to the Indian subcontinent. Measurements

Magnetic polarity stratig- raphy of the drill core indicates that the top of the section is in the Cretaceous long nor- mal polarity interval, 26 m above the re- verse polarity zone correlative to polarity chron CM0. Tremolada Dipartimento di Scienze della Terra, Universita Á di Milano, 20133 Milano, Italy ABSTRACT Lower Cretaceous mainly white and/or gray pelagic cherty limestones have been sampled in the APTICORE drill core and in the adjacent outcrop at Cismon, South- ern Alps, Italy. Magnetic polarity stratig- raphy of the drill core indicates that the top of the section is in the Cretaceous long nor- mal polarity interval, 26 m above the re- verse polarity zone correlative to polarity chron CM0. The base of the drilled section, at a stratigraphic depth of 116.71 m, is in a reverse polarity zone correlative to CM9. The coeval stratigraphic interval has been sampled in the adjacent outcrop in order to tie the drill core record to the outcrop. The correlation of polarity zones to polarity chrons is aided by the know

which is to document the record of mid-Cretaceous greenhouse cli- matic warming (Erba and Larson, 1998). The need for a continuous, uninterrupted section for biostratigraphy, cyclostratigraphy, and geochemical studies led to the drilling of a single 131.8-m-long bore hole through the middle Aptian to lower Hauterivian section (Erba and Larson, 1998; Erba et al., 1999). Drilling was carried out in December 1995 and January 1996. The core recovery was es- sentially 100% with a core diameter of 11 cm. The hole was then reamed to 20 cm diameter for geophysical logging. The preliminary lithologic description of cores was carried out at the drill site (see Erba and Larson, 1998; Erba et al., 1999). Cores were sectioned in 1 m lengths, packed in wooden crates, and transported to Milan for additional lithologic description, whole-core magnetic susceptibility measurements, core splitting, and subsampling. Ion microprobe U–Pb dating of zircon and baddeleyite indicates that the MDS was emplaced at 755± 3M a( 9 5% conﬁdence interval ) and palaeomagnetic results conﬁrm that the swarm is equivalent in age to dykes of the Northampton Inlier. A positive contact test between an MDS dyke and an older dolerite sill indicates that the MDS magnetisation dates from the time of dyke emplacement and cooling at 755 Ma. Combining new palaeomagnetic data for eight MDS dykes with previous results for six Northampton dykes yields a palaeopole for Australia at 135 ° E, 46° N( A95=4° ). The MDS palaeopole lies 30 ° away from the 780 to 740 Ma APW path segment for Laurentia, indicating that, if the Rodinia reconstruction is correct, breakup between Australia and Laurentia occurred prior to 755 Ma. Ion microprobe U–Pb dating of zircon and baddeleyite indicates that the MDS was emplaced at 755± 3M a( 9 5% conﬁdence interval ) and palaeomagnetic results conﬁrm that the swarm is equivalent in age to dykes of the Northampton Inlier. A positive contact test between an MDS dyke and an older dolerite sill indicates that the MDS magnetisation dates from the time of dyke emplacement and cooling at 755 Ma. Combining new palaeomagnetic data for eight MDS dykes with previous results for six Northampton dykes yields a palaeopole for Australia at 135 ° E, 46° N( A95=4° ). The MDS palaeopole lies 30 ° away from the 780 to 740 Ma APW path segment for Laurentia, indicating that, if the Rodinia reconstruction is correct, breakup between Australia and Laurentia occurred prior to 755 Ma. Li * Tectonics Special Research Centre, Department of Geology and Geophysics, The University of Western Australia, Nedlands, W A 6907, Australia Abstract An interpreted primary magnetic remanence that passed a fold test has been revealed from six sampling sites in the pink ‘cap dolomite’ of the Neoproterozoic Walsh Tillite, southern Kimberley, northwestern Australia. A palaeomagnetic pole ( WTC ) at (21.5 ° S, 282.4° E) with dp =12.2° and dm=15.4° , based on results of the ﬁve best sites, gives a palaeolatitude of 45 ± 12° for the sampling region, and ca 25 ± 12° for the Adelaide Fold Belt where two Neoproterozoic glaciations occur. This palaeopole falls 58° away from the Marinoan glaciation (the Elatina Formation) pole, and the palaeolatitude for the region studied is around 30 ° higher than that predicted by the Marinoan and younger Neoproterozoic poles from Australia. If the WTC pole is accepted as a palaeopole at the end of the Walsh glaciation, the Walsh Tillite is thus likely to be of Sturtian (ca 770–750 Ma) rather than Marinoan age. A comparison of the revised late Mesoproterozoic to Neoproterozoic apparent polar wander path (APWP) for East Gondwana with that of Laurentia suggests that supercontinent Rodinia broke apart by about 750 Ma, after the Sturtian glaciation. B2, PAGES 2805-2815, FEBRUARY 10, 2000 New constraints on the Upper Permian and Lower Triassic geomagnetic polarity timescale from the A badeh section (central Iran) Yves Gallet, 1 Leopold Krystyn, 2 Jean Besse, and Luc-Emmanuel Ricou 1 1 Abdolah Saidi, 3 Abstract. We present the magnetostratigraphy of the Abadeh section (central Iran). Thermal demagnetization shows two magnetic components: one at low unblocking temperatures, which corresponds to a present day-field direction, and another at high temperatures. This second component, which contains both polarities, is interpreted as a primary magnetization acquired during sediment deposition at a paleolatitude of about 7.7øS. A sequence of 14 magnetic polarity zones is obtained in the intervals during the Upper Dzhulfian-Lower Changhsingian (Upper Permian) and during the Griesbachian (Lower Triassic). Combining data from south China, Canada, Pakistan, and Iran, we propose a composite (but still uncomplete) Upper Permian and Lower Triassic geomagnetic polarity timescale. 1. One group (A) preserves stable single thermoremanent magnetizations (TRM) with large westerly deflected declinations. Determination of the timing and extent of rotational events based on reliable paleomagnetic data and radiometric ages is essential to clarify the tectonic history of the Eurasian plate margin. In this article, we present a paleomagnetic and chro- nologic study of the Kurihashi Granodiorite near the Pacific coast of northeast Japan. A preliminary investigation [Itoh et al., 1998a] showed that the plutonic rock can be divided into two groups based on paleomagnetic data: one sample group (A) preserves a stable single component of thermoremanent magnetization (TRM), and the other sample group (B) has two or three distinct components of remanence. The mean char- acteristic direction of the TRMs of group A has a large west- erly deflection (Figure 2) consistent with other directions re- ported from Cretaceous plutonic rocks in northeast Japan [Ito and Tokieda, 1986]. It is expected therefore that analysis of the multicomponent remanent magnetization will indicate the ro- tational process in our study area. In addition, fission track thermochronology will provide us with the timing of rema- nence acquisition events, namely, the initial cooling of the plutonic body and later thermal event that is anticipated from fracture-filling mineral assemblages lAmario et al., 1998]. Determination of the timing and extent of rotational events based on reliable paleomagnetic data and radiometric ages is essential to clarify the tectonic history of the Eurasian plate margin. In this article, we present a paleomagnetic and chro- nologic study of the Kurihashi Granodiorite near the Pacific coast of northeast Japan. A preliminary investigation [Itoh et al., 1998a] showed that the plutonic rock can be divided into two groups based on paleomagnetic data: one sample group (A) preserves a stable single component of thermoremanent magnetization (TRM), and the other sample group (B) has two or three distinct components of remanence. The mean char- acteristic direction of the TRMs of group A has a large west- erly deflection (Figure 2) consistent with other directions re- ported from Cretaceous plutonic rocks in northeast Japan [Ito and Tokieda, 1986]. It is expected therefore that analysis of the multicomponent remanent magnetization will indicate the ro- tational process in our study area. In addition, fission track thermochronology will provide us with the timing of rema- nence acquisition events, namely, the initial cooling of the plutonic body and later thermal event that is anticipated from fracture-filling mineral assemblages lAmario et al., 1998]. Samples from the Late Cretaceous Kurihashi Granodiorite on the Pacific coast of northeast Japan are divided into two groups based on paleomagnetic data. One group (A) preserves stable single thermoremanent magnetizations (TRM) with large westerly deflected declinations. The other group (B) has two or three distinct components of natural remanent magnetization (NRM): components with high, middle, and low unblocking temperatures show westerly declinations (nearly identical with the stable TRM directions of group A), as well as northerly and easterly declinations. Rock magnetic experiments indicate that the dominant magnetic mineral of both groups is Ti-poor titanomagnetite. Group A samples contain superparamagnetic (SP) titanomagnetite because they show a frequency dependence with the initial susceptibility measurements: Hysteresis parameters of group B samples are consistent with a mixture of single-domain (SD) and multidomain (MD) grains. Electron microscopy confirms the presence of MD size magnetite in the group B samples.
